 Supreme Court Upholds Distribution Licensee's Appeal in Electricity Theft Assessment Case — High Court's Directions Found Erroneous. Court Clarifies Distinction Between Theft and Unauthorized Use of Electricity Under Sections 135 and 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
 Admin 
 2026-10-27 05:21:21 
 11 
 Share This 
 Article: 
 Font size: 
 Print 
 Case Note & Summary
 The judgment involved two civil appeals concerning the assessment of electricity theft under the Electricity Act, 2003. The first appeal arose from a notice issued to M/s Vaibhav Metal Crusher for theft of electricity, demanding a total of Rs. 92,99,077.55. The respondent challenged this notice in the High Court, which allowed a partial deposit for reconnection of supply. The distribution licensee appealed against this interim order, arguing that the demand was for theft, which does not require prior hearing. The High Court later directed the respondent to file objections to the notice, which the appellant contested. The second appeal involved Jamanbhai Nanajibhai Bhuva, who similarly challenged a supplementary bill for theft. The High Court had directed a partial deposit for reconnection, which the appellant also contested. The Supreme Court analyzed the provisions of the Electricity Act, particularly Sections 135, 126, and 127, and the implications of the High Court's orders. It concluded that the High Court erred in allowing objections and directing reconnection based on partial payment, emphasizing that theft assessments are distinct and governed by specific provisions that do not permit such remedies. The court ultimately upheld the appellant's position regarding the legal framework governing electricity theft assessments and the rights of consumers in such cases.
 Headnote
 A) Electricity Law - Theft of Electricity - Provisional Assessment and Consumer Rights - Electricity Act, 2003, Sections 135, 126, 127 - The court examined the legality of supplementary bills issued for electricity theft and the consumer's right to appeal against such assessments. It held that the High Court's direction to allow objections and restore supply on partial payment was erroneous as the assessment for theft is distinct from unauthorized use and is subject to different legal provisions (Paras 12-30).

 Final Decision
 The Supreme Court upheld the appeals of the distribution licensees, ruling that the High Court's orders allowing objections and directing reconnection based on partial payment were erroneous. The court clarified that assessments for theft of electricity are distinct from those for unauthorized use and governed by specific provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003.

 Nature of Litigation
 Civil appeals regarding assessment of electricity theft and related orders from the High Court.
 Remedy Sought
 The distribution licensees sought to challenge the High Court's interim orders allowing partial payment for reconnection.
 Filing Reason
 The respondents challenged the supplementary bills issued for alleged theft of electricity.
 Previous Decisions
 The High Court had allowed partial deposits for reconnection and directed the filing of objections to the supplementary bills.
 Issues
 Whether the High Court erred in allowing objections to supplementary bills raised for electricity theft.
Whether the High Court's direction to restore supply upon partial payment was legally justified.
 Submissions/Arguments
 The appellant argued that the demand for theft of electricity does not require prior hearing and that the High Court erred in allowing objections.
The respondents contended that the third proviso to Section 135 allows for restoration of supply upon deposit of assessed amounts.
 Ratio Decidendi
 The court established that the assessment for theft of electricity under Section 135 is distinct from unauthorized use under Section 126, and the consumer does not have the right to appeal against provisional assessments for theft.
 Judgment Excerpts
 The court examined the legality of supplementary bills issued for electricity theft.
The High Court's direction to allow objections and restore supply on partial payment was erroneous.
 Procedural History
 The appeals arose from interim orders of the High Court allowing partial deposits for reconnection of electricity supply in cases of alleged theft.
